concept: Answer Verification (self-consistency, verification chains, hallucination detection, attribution/factuality scoring, LLM-as-judge, iterative refinement limits, multi-agent debate, process/outcome verifiers, calibration and confidence elicitation, rubric evaluation, tool-grounded verification)
summary:
Answer verification is the pipeline stage that decides whether a candidate output (answer, plan, code, spec edit, incident summary) is correct, grounded and safe to release, and if not, what to do about it: select a better candidate, repair it with evidence, abstain, or escalate. The literature converges on four families of signal. (1) Agreement across samples: Self-Consistency (Wang et al., ICLR 2023) shows majority vote over ~40 sampled reasoning paths adds +17.9 points on GSM8K and that the agreement fraction is itself a calibrated confidence; Universal Self-Consistency (Chen et al. 2023) extends this to free-form outputs by letting the LLM pick the most consistent of 8 candidates, and Adaptive-Consistency (Aggarwal et al., EMNLP 2023) cuts sample budgets up to 7.9x with <0.1% accuracy loss via early stopping. The same disagreement signal, computed over meaning clusters, becomes semantic entropy (Kuhn et al., ICLR 2023; Farquhar et al., Nature 2024, AUROC 0.790 vs 0.69-0.70 for baselines with 10 samples) and SelfCheckGPT (Manakul et al., EMNLP 2023, 93.4 AUC-PR for non-factual sentence detection with 20 samples). (2) Evidence-grounded claim checking: FActScore (Min et al., EMNLP 2023) decomposes text into atomic facts and scores the supported fraction with <2% estimator error; RARR (Gao et al., ACL 2023), FacTool (Chern et al. 2023) and Chain-of-Verification (Dhuliawala et al. 2023) generate verification questions, retrieve or execute tools, and minimally revise (CoVe factor+revise lifts biography FActScore 55.9 -> 71.4; RARR preserves intent >90% while raising attribution ~9-11 points). (3) Learned or prompted verifiers: Cobbe et al. (2021) show a 6B verifier reranking 100 samples beats a 30x larger finetuned model; Lightman et al. (2023) show process supervision (PRM) reaches 78.2% on MATH vs 72.4% ORM and 69.6% majority vote at N=1860; Math-Shepherd, PAVs and Generative Verifiers remove the human-labelling bottleneck and make verifiers scale with test-time compute (Snell et al. 2024: >4x compute-efficiency over best-of-N). LLM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al., NeurIPS 2023) achieves 85% agreement with human experts (human-human 81%) but exhibits position bias (GPT-4 only 65% order-consistent), verbosity bias (91% failure on repetition attacks for GPT-3.5/Claude-v1) and self-preference (Panickssery et al. 2024). (4) Calibration: RLHF models verbalize better-calibrated confidence than their token probabilities (Tian et al., EMNLP 2023, ~50% relative ECE reduction with top-k verbalization) but remain overconfident (Xiong et al., ICLR 2024), so confidence should be fused from consistency plus verbalized estimates and used for routing, not trusted alone.

The most important negative result for production design is that intrinsic self-correction does not work: Huang et al. (ICLR 2024) show GPT-4 drops from 95.5% to 89.0% on GSM8K after two rounds of unassisted self-correction and that multi-agent debate underperforms plain self-consistency at equal sample budgets (83.0% vs 88.2% at 9 responses); Self-Refine's math gain was 0-0.2 points because the model declared "everything looks good" 94% of the time; CRITIC's ablation shows self-critique without tools gives negligible or negative gains; Olausson et al. (ICLR 2024) show code self-repair is "often modest" and bottlenecked by feedback quality; Kamoi et al. (TACL 2024) find no successful prompted self-correction outside tasks with reliable external feedback. The state of the art is therefore a verification component built around external or statistical evidence (execution, retrieval, agreement, trained verifiers), with LLM judgment used only in debiased, rubric-anchored, reference-guided form, with explicit confidence gating and abstention, and with the budget allocated adaptively per query.

papers.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
papers.authors: Xuezhi Wang, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans, Quoc Le, Ed Chi, Sharan Narang, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Denny Zhou
papers.citation_signal: 7,953 citations (Semantic Scholar, Oct 2026); ICLR 2023; the canonical sampling-based verification baseline
papers.key_contribution: Replaces greedy CoT decoding with sampling 40 diverse reasoning paths (T=0.7, top-k 40 for PaLM-540B; T=0.7 for GPT-3) and majority-voting the final answer. Gains over CoT: GSM8K +17.9 (PaLM-540B 56.5 -> 74.4; code-davinci-002 60.1 -> 78.0), SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-c +3.9. Accuracy saturates quickly (5-10 paths capture most of the gain) and the fraction of samples agreeing with the majority is highly correlated with accuracy, so it doubles as a confidence score.
papers.design_implication: Make k-sample majority vote the default verification primitive for any task with an extractable, normalizable answer (numbers, labels, SQL results, test outcomes). Use the agreement ratio as a free confidence signal to drive routing and abstention. Start at k=5-10 and only scale to 20-40 for hard, high-stakes queries.

papers.title: Universal Self-Consistency for Large Language Model Generation
papers.authors: Xinyun Chen, Renat Aksitov, Uri Alon, Jie Ren, Kefan Xiao, Pengcheng Yin, Sushant Prakash, Charles Sutton, Xuezhi Wang, Denny Zhou
papers.citation_signal: Widely cited follow-up to Self-Consistency from the same group; adopted in practice for free-form voting
papers.key_contribution: Lets the LLM select the most consistent answer among 8 sampled candidates instead of requiring an extractable answer. Matches SC on math (PaLM 2-L GSM8K: SC 90.4 vs USC 90.2; MATH 37.9 vs 37.4) and matches execution-based voting on code without running code (BIRD-SQL 45.6 vs 45.5; ARCADE 30.3 vs 30.1), and improves free-form tasks where SC does not apply (GovReport ROUGE-1 38.8 -> 40.2; TruthfulQA GPT-judge 62.1 -> 67.7 for PaLM 2-L). Limitations: candidates are bounded by context length, no confidence estimate is produced, gains plateau after ~5 samples on summarization and GSM8K dropped at 16 samples.
papers.design_implication: Use USC as the aggregation fallback when answers cannot be canonicalized (summaries, specs, incident narratives, design rationales). Cap candidates at 5-8, randomize their order, and pair it with a separate confidence estimator since USC yields none.

papers.title: Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning and Coding with LLMs
papers.authors: Pranjal Aggarwal, Aman Madaan, Yiming Yang, Mausam
papers.citation_signal: EMNLP 2023 main; standard reference for cost-aware self-consistency
papers.key_contribution: Allocates samples per question with a lightweight stopping criterion based on the agreement observed so far (posterior probability that the current majority is stable). Across 17 reasoning and code datasets and three LLMs, it reduces the sample budget by up to 7.9x with an average accuracy drop below 0.1%.
papers.design_implication: Never use a fixed k in production: sample sequentially (or in small parallel batches) and stop when the majority's posterior stability exceeds a threshold (~0.95). This turns verification cost from O(k_max) per query into a budget concentrated on genuinely ambiguous queries.

papers.title: Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in Large Language Models
papers.authors: Shehzaad Dhuliawala, Mojtaba Komeili, Jing Xu, Roberta Raileanu, Xian Li, Asli Celikyilmaz, Jason Weston
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (Meta AI); Findings of ACL 2024
papers.citation_signal: Hundreds of citations; widely adopted verification-prompting pattern
papers.key_contribution: Four steps: draft baseline response; plan verification questions; execute verifications (joint, 2-step, factored, factor+revise variants); generate final verified response. With Llama 65B: Wikidata list precision 0.17 -> 0.36 (2-step); Wiki-Category 0.12 -> 0.22 (factored); MultiSpanQA F1 0.39 -> 0.48 (factored); biography FActScore 55.9 -> 63.7 (factored) -> 71.4 (factor+revise). Factored variants beat joint because answering verification questions without the draft in context prevents the model from copying its own hallucinations. Average fact count fell 16.6 -> 12.3 (precision gained partly by dropping claims).
papers.design_implication: Implement verification questions as isolated calls that do not see the original draft (factored), then an explicit cross-check step (factor+revise). Track recall/claim-count alongside precision so the component is not rewarded for simply deleting content.

papers.title: Verify-and-Edit: A Knowledge-Enhanced Chain-of-Thought Framework
papers.authors: Ruochen Zhao, Xingxuan Li, Shafiq Joty, Chengwei Qin, Lidong Bing
papers.citation_signal: Several hundred citations; one of the first retrieval-grounded CoT post-editing frameworks
papers.key_contribution: Post-edits CoT rationales with external knowledge: self-consistency agreement is used to decide which questions are uncertain (low agreement), then verification questions are generated, retrieved against (search/Wikipedia), and the rationale is edited before re-deriving the answer. Reports accuracy improvements on multiple open-domain QA tasks with GPT-3.
papers.design_implication: Use agreement as a trigger: only run expensive retrieval-grounded editing on low-consistency outputs. This is the canonical 'uncertainty-gated verification' pattern and directly ties the verification component to hybrid retrieval.

papers.title: Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models (Self-Ask)
papers.authors: Ofir Press, Muru Zhang, Sewon Min, Ludwig Schmidt, Noah A. Smith, Mike Lewis
papers.citation_signal: Widely cited; Self-Ask is a standard decomposition-plus-check prompt pattern
papers.key_contribution: Defines the compositionality gap (sub-questions right, composition wrong), shows it does not shrink with scale across GPT-3 sizes, and introduces self-ask: the model explicitly poses and answers follow-up questions before the final answer, which beats chain-of-thought; the structured follow-ups can be routed to a search engine, further improving accuracy.
papers.design_implication: Structure verification as explicit sub-questions that can be dispatched to tools/retrieval rather than one monolithic 'is this correct?' prompt. The explicit structure also makes verification traces auditable.

papers.title: SelfCheckGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection for Generative Large Language Models
papers.authors: Potsawee Manakul, Adian Liusie, Mark J. F. Gales
papers.citation_signal: EMNLP 2023 main; >1,000 citations; standard black-box hallucination baseline
papers.key_contribution: Samples N=20 stochastic responses (T=1.0) and checks each sentence of the main (T=0, beam) response against them with BERTScore, QA, n-gram, NLI, or an LLM prompt. On WikiBio GPT-3 passages: non-factual sentence AUC-PR 93.42 (Prompt), 92.50 (NLI) vs 87.51 for the best grey-box token-probability baseline and 72.96 random; passage-level Pearson 78.32 (Prompt) vs 57.83 baseline.
papers.design_implication: When token logprobs are unavailable (API models) or untrustworthy, sentence-level consistency against samples is the best zero-resource hallucination detector. The NLI variant (DeBERTa) is nearly as good as the LLM-prompt variant at a fraction of the cost and should be the default scorer.

papers.title: Semantic Uncertainty: Linguistic Invariances for Uncertainty Estimation in Natural Language Generation
papers.authors: Lorenz Kuhn, Yarin Gal, Sebastian Farquhar
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2023 spotlight; >1,000 citations; precursor to the Nature paper
papers.key_contribution: Introduces semantic entropy: cluster sampled generations by meaning (bidirectional entailment) and compute entropy over clusters rather than surface strings. Unsupervised, single-model, no modification to off-the-shelf LLMs; more predictive of accuracy than token-level entropy baselines on QA.
papers.design_implication: Meaning-level clustering is required for any uncertainty metric over free text; surface-level agreement under-counts agreement among paraphrases and over-estimates uncertainty.

papers.title: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy
papers.authors: Sebastian Farquhar, Jannik Kossen, Lorenz Kuhn, Yarin Gal
papers.citation_signal: 1,859 citations (Semantic Scholar, Oct 2026); Nature
papers.key_contribution: Targets confabulations (arbitrary, incorrect generations). Uses 10 sampled generations, clusters them by bidirectional entailment (GPT-3.5 or DeBERTa-large-MNLI), and computes entropy over clusters; a discrete variant needs no token probabilities and performs similarly. Averaged over 30 task-model combinations (TriviaQA, SQuAD, BioASQ, NQ-Open, SVAMP; LLaMA 2 Chat, Falcon Instruct, Mistral Instruct), AUROC 0.790 vs naive entropy 0.691, P(True) 0.698, embedding regression 0.687. Extends to paragraphs by decomposing into factoids, generating questions per factoid, and averaging semantic entropy; beats self-check and P(True) baselines on AUROC and AURAC.
papers.design_implication: Implement discrete semantic entropy as the standard uncertainty score for black-box models: N=10 samples, NLI-based bidirectional entailment clustering, entropy over cluster counts. For long outputs, apply per atomic claim and aggregate; use the score to trigger retrieval verification or abstention.

papers.title: FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation
papers.authors: Sewon Min, Kalpesh Krishna, Xinxi Lyu, Mike Lewis, Wen-tau Yih, Pang Wei Koh, Mohit Iyyer, Luke Zettlemoyer, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
papers.citation_signal: 1,823 citations (Semantic Scholar, Oct 2026); EMNLP 2023 main; pip-installable standard
papers.key_contribution: Decomposes a generation into atomic facts, labels each Supported/Not-supported against a knowledge source, and reports the supported fraction over non-abstaining responses. Human FActScore on biographies: InstructGPT ~42.5%, ChatGPT ~58.3%, PerplexityAI ~71.5%; accuracy collapses for rare entities (ChatGPT ~80% -> 16%) and for facts later in the text. Automated estimator (decompose -> retrieve Wikipedia -> LM support judgement, optionally plus nonparametric probability) has <2% error vs humans; evaluating 6,500 generations would have cost ~$26K with humans. FActScore is precision-only, so it must be reported with abstention rate and average fact count.
papers.design_implication: Build the attribution scorer as decompose -> retrieve -> entail per atomic claim; always emit three numbers (supported fraction, claim count, abstention) so the pipeline cannot game precision by saying less. Expect lower factuality on long-tail entities (rare part numbers, obscure standards clauses) and route those to retrieval.

papers.title: RARR: Researching and Revising What Language Models Say, Using Language Models
papers.authors: Luyu Gao, Zhuyun Dai, Panupong Pasupat, Anthony Chen, Arun Tejasvi Chaganty, Yicheng Fan, Vincent Y. Zhao, Ni Lao, Hongrae Lee, Da-Cheng Juan, Kelvin Guu
papers.citation_signal: ACL 2023; several hundred citations; reference architecture for post-hoc attribution and revision
papers.key_contribution: Research stage: generate covering questions, web-search each (5 pages/query), keep best snippet. Revision stage: an agreement model flags evidence that contradicts the text; an edit model revises only then, and oversized edits are rejected. Attribution report: up to 5 snippets. Auto-AIS attribution rises NQ 45.6 -> 54.9, SQA 37.6 -> 45.1, QReCC 18.8 -> 29.4 while preserving intent >90% of the time; baselines (EFEC, LaMDA) get higher attribution only by rewriting (preservation 4-34%), giving RARR the best F1_AP (57.0 / 45.9 / 41.5).
papers.design_implication: Separate 'agreement check' from 'edit' and only edit on contradiction; enforce an edit-size budget (Levenshtein/preservation) so verification does not silently rewrite the author's intent. Emit the attribution report as a first-class artifact.

papers.title: FacTool: Factuality Detection in Generative AI -- A Tool Augmented Framework for Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Scenarios
papers.authors: I-Chun Chern, Steffi Chern, Shiqi Chen, Weizhe Yuan, Kehua Feng, Chunting Zhou, Junxian He, Graham Neubig, Pengfei Liu
papers.citation_signal: Several hundred citations; released as open-source library and ChatGPT plugin
papers.key_contribution: Five-step, task/domain-agnostic framework: claim extraction, query generation, tool querying, evidence collection, agreement verification. Tools per domain: Google Search (KB-QA), Python interpreter running generated tests with majority-vote pseudo-golden outputs (code), interpreter re-computing each arithmetic step (math), Google Scholar metadata check (literature). Claim/response F1 with GPT-4: KB-QA 89.1/71.8, code 92.1, math 99.0/80.4, sci-lit 95.2/94.7, versus Self-Check (GPT-4) 86.6/57.1, 85.3, 95.8/70.6 and 36.7/21.5 respectively; self-check has lower precision and misses errors.
papers.design_implication: This is the template for a pluggable verifier: a claim-type router that dispatches each claim to a domain tool (search, code runner, calculator, catalog/API lookup) then runs a single agreement step. Self-check without tools is the weakest arm and should not be the only verifier for any factual claim.

papers.title: Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations (ALCE)
papers.authors: Tianyu Gao, Howard Yen, Jiatong Yu, Danqi Chen
papers.citation_signal: EMNLP 2023 main; standard citation-quality benchmark (princeton-nlp/ALCE)
papers.key_contribution: First benchmark for automatic evaluation of LLM citations (fluency, correctness, citation recall/precision via NLI), shown to correlate strongly with human judgments. Even the best models lack complete citation support 50% of the time on ELI5; improvements need better retrievers, long-context models and multi-source synthesis.
papers.design_implication: Score citation recall and precision separately with an NLI entailment model over (claim, cited passage) pairs; make 'every sentence with a factual claim must be entailed by at least one cited chunk' a hard gate for RAG outputs.

papers.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
papers.authors: Lianmin Zheng, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ying Sheng, Siyuan Zhuang, Zhanghao Wu, Yonghao Zhuang, Zi Lin, Zhuohan Li, Dacheng Li, Eric P. Xing, Hao Zhang, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Ion Stoica
papers.citation_signal: Several thousand citations; the defining LLM-as-a-judge paper; basis of Chatbot Arena
papers.key_contribution: GPT-4 pairwise judgments agree with human experts 85% (first and second turn, non-tie), exceeding human-human agreement (81-82%). Documents biases: position bias (order-consistency GPT-4 65.0%, GPT-3.5 46.2%, Claude-v1 23.8%), verbosity bias (repetitive-list attack fooled Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 91.3% of the time, GPT-4 8.7%), self-enhancement (GPT-4 ~+10%, Claude-v1 ~+25% win rate on own outputs, inconclusive), and limited math/reasoning grading (default prompt failed 14/20 math cases; CoT 6/20; reference-guided 3/20). Mitigations: swap positions and count only consistent wins, few-shot judge (65 -> 77.5% consistency at ~4x cost), CoT, reference-guided grading.
papers.design_implication: Any LLM judge in the component must run position-swapped, use reference-guided grading whenever a reference or executed result exists, be a different model family from the generator, and be length-controlled. Treat the judge as a noisy ~85%-agreement sensor, not ground truth.

papers.title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
papers.authors: Peiyi Wang, Lei Li, Liang Chen, Zefan Cai, Dawei Zhu, Binghuai Lin, Yunbo Cao, Qi Liu, Tianyu Liu, Zhifang Sui
papers.citation_signal: Several hundred citations; the standard reference for position-bias calibration
papers.key_contribution: Shows rankings can be flipped by candidate order: Vicuna-13B 'beat' ChatGPT on 66/80 queries when order favored it. Proposes Multiple Evidence Calibration (generate evidence before scoring), Balanced Position Calibration (aggregate across both orders) and Human-in-the-Loop Calibration using a balanced position diversity entropy to flag hard cases for humans.
papers.design_implication: Use order-swap aggregation by default and compute the position-diversity entropy as an escalation signal: items whose verdict depends on order go to a human or a stronger verifier.

papers.title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
papers.authors: Arjun Panickssery, Samuel R. Bowman, Shi Feng
papers.citation_signal: Widely cited bias study; informs judge-selection practice
papers.key_contribution: GPT-4 and Llama 2 distinguish their own outputs from others with non-trivial accuracy out of the box; fine-tuning reveals a linear relationship between self-recognition ability and self-preference bias, with controlled experiments indicating the link is causal rather than confounded.
papers.design_implication: Never let the same model (or family) that generated a candidate be the sole judge of it; use cross-family judges or non-LLM verifiers (execution, retrieval entailment) for the final gate.

papers.title: Length-Controlled AlpacaEval: A Simple Way to Debias Automatic Evaluators
papers.authors: Yann Dubois, Balázs Galambosi, Percy Liang, Tatsunori B. Hashimoto
papers.citation_signal: COLM 2024; adopted as the default AlpacaEval leaderboard metric
papers.key_contribution: Fits a GLM predicting judge preference from length difference and other features, then reports the counterfactual preference at zero length difference. Makes the metric robust to verbosity manipulation and raises Spearman correlation with Chatbot Arena from 0.94 to 0.98.
papers.design_implication: Log output lengths and apply a length-controlled correction (or explicit length-normalized rubric) to any pairwise judge score used for selection among candidates.

papers.title: G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment
papers.authors: Yang Liu, Dan Iter, Yichong Xu, Shuohang Wang, Ruochen Xu, Chenguang Zhu
papers.citation_signal: EMNLP 2023; >1,000 citations; widely implemented in eval libraries
papers.key_contribution: Rubric-based LLM evaluation: auto-generated CoT evaluation steps plus a form-filling score, with final score computed as the probability-weighted sum over score tokens to reduce ties. GPT-4 G-Eval reaches Spearman 0.514 with humans on SummEval, beating prior metrics by a large margin. The authors flag a bias toward LLM-generated text.
papers.design_implication: Rubric-driven scoring should use explicit criteria, decomposed evaluation steps and probability-weighted (or multi-sample averaged) scores, never a single raw integer; keep a human-anchored calibration set because judges prefer LLM-style text.

papers.title: Prometheus: Inducing Fine-grained Evaluation Capability in Language Models
papers.authors: Seungone Kim, Jamin Shin, Yejin Cho, Joel Jang, Shayne Longpre, Hwaran Lee, Sangdoo Yun, Seongjin Shin, Sungdong Kim, James Thorne, Minjoon Seo
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2024; widely used open evaluator model
papers.key_contribution: Open 13B evaluator trained on Feedback Collection (1K rubrics, 20K instructions, 100K GPT-4 feedback). With a reference answer and rubric, Pearson 0.897 with humans across 45 custom rubrics vs GPT-4 0.882 and ChatGPT 0.392; top open reward-model accuracy on HHH Alignment and MT-Bench Human Judgment.
papers.design_implication: A fine-tuned open judge given (rubric, reference) can replace proprietary judges for cost, versioning and data-residency reasons; the key enablers are the reference answer and a fine-grained rubric, so the component should always surface both to the judge when available.

papers.title: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
papers.authors: Aman Madaan, Niket Tandon, Prakhar Gupta, Skyler Hallinan, Luyu Gao, Sarah Wiegreffe, Uri Alon, Nouha Dziri, Shrimai Prabhumoye, Yiming Yang, Shashank Gupta, Bodhisattwa Prasad Majumder, Katherine Hermann, Sean Welleck, Amir Yazdanbakhsh, Peter Clark
papers.citation_signal: Several thousand citations; defining iterative-refinement paper
papers.key_contribution: Generate -> feedback -> refine loop with one model, up to 4 iterations, stopping on a fixed step or a stop indicator in the feedback. ~20 points absolute average gain over 7 tasks (e.g., Dialogue +49.2 GPT-4, Sentiment +32.4, Code readability +28.8, Code optimization +8.7) but GSM8K gains of 0 to +0.2 because ChatGPT said 'everything looks good' on 94% of instances; oracle feedback gave +4.8. Specific actionable feedback matters: generic feedback dropped Sentiment Reversal 43.2 -> 31.2.
papers.design_implication: Iterative refinement is a valid stage only for tasks with subjective or stylistic quality dimensions and when feedback is concrete; for correctness-critical tasks the feedback must come from an external verifier. Cap at 2-4 iterations with an explicit stop indicator.

papers.title: CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
papers.authors: Zhibin Gou, Zhihong Shao, Yeyun Gong, Yelong Shen, Yujiu Yang, Nan Duan, Weizhu Chen
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2024; >700 citations
papers.key_contribution: Verify-then-correct loop where critiques are grounded in tool outputs (search, Python interpreter, toxicity API). Free-form QA F1 +5.6 (text-davinci-003) and +7.7 (ChatGPT) over CoT; math program synthesis ~+7.0 average on ChatGPT (TabMWP +14.0); toxicity probability 0.192 -> 0.040. Critical ablation: without tools, QA gains are -0.03 to +2.33 F1, math is unstable and toxicity worsens (0.192 -> 0.223), so external feedback is essential.
papers.design_implication: Every correction loop must be fed by an external signal (execution result, retrieved evidence, API verdict). Build 'critique without tools' only as a cheap triage step, never as the correction authority.

papers.title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
papers.authors: Jie Huang, Xinyun Chen, Swaroop Mishra, Huaixiu Steven Zheng, Adams Wei Yu, Xinying Song, Denny Zhou
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2024; >800 citations; the key negative result on intrinsic self-correction
papers.key_contribution: Intrinsic self-correction (no oracle) lowers accuracy: GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0 over two rounds; GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1; Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 -> 36.5. Earlier positive results relied on oracle correctness labels (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3 with oracle). Multi-agent debate underperforms self-consistency at equal budget on GSM8K (6 responses: debate 83.2 vs SC 85.3; 9 responses: 83.0 vs 88.2), attributing debate's gains to consistency rather than correction.
papers.design_implication: Do not deploy 'review your answer and fix mistakes' prompts as a verification mechanism for reasoning tasks; they introduce regressions. Spend the same budget on sampling plus voting or on tool/verifier-grounded checks, and benchmark debate against SC at matched cost before adopting it.

papers.title: LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
papers.authors: Gladys Tyen, Hassan Mansoor, Victor Cărbune, Peter Chen, Tony Mak
papers.citation_signal: ACL 2024 Findings; releases BIG-Bench Mistake
papers.key_contribution: State-of-the-art LLMs struggle to locate logical mistakes even in unambiguous cases, but when given the ground-truth mistake location (backtracking setup) they improve across 5 reasoning tasks. A small classifier trained on out-of-domain data finds mistakes better than prompting a large model.
papers.design_implication: Split verification into localization and repair. Invest in cheap, trained error-localizers (small classifiers, PRMs, test failures, retrieval contradictions) and pass the precise location to the repair step; generic 'find your error' prompts are the weak link.

papers.title: Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
papers.authors: Theo X. Olausson, Jeevana Priya Inala, Chenglong Wang, Jianfeng Gao, Armando Solar-Lezama
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2024; standard reference on cost-accounted code self-repair
papers.key_contribution: Accounting for repair cost, GPT-4 self-repair on APPS beats the no-repair baseline by at most ~8% (10 initial samples + 1 repair = 1.05x baseline pass@20; 2 samples + 10 repairs = 0.97x). GPT-3.5 gains are marginal. Repair success rises 4.7% -> 11.5% when GPT-4 supplies feedback for GPT-3.5, and 33.3% -> 52.6% with human feedback, showing the bottleneck is feedback quality.
papers.design_implication: For code verification, prefer breadth (more initial samples filtered by tests) over depth (many repair rounds); when repairing, feed compiler/test output and, if available, a stronger model's diagnosis rather than the generator's own critique.

papers.title: When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
papers.authors: Ryo Kamoi, Yusen Zhang, Nan Zhang, Jiawei Han, Rui Zhang
papers.citation_signal: TACL (top journal); the authoritative synthesis on self-correction
papers.key_contribution: Categorizes self-correction research questions and proposes an experiment-design checklist. Findings: no surveyed work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs except on tasks particularly suited to it; self-correction works when reliable external feedback exists; large-scale fine-tuning can enable it. Many prior positive results used unfair baselines or oracle information.
papers.design_implication: Make 'reliable external feedback available?' the routing condition for any correction loop; where it is absent, use selection (best-of-N, voting) or abstain rather than refine.

papers.title: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
papers.authors: Yilun Du, Shuang Li, Antonio Torralba, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Igor Mordatch
papers.citation_signal: Over a thousand citations; defining multi-agent debate paper
papers.key_contribution: Multiple LLM instances answer, read each other's answers, and revise over rounds (3 agents, 2 rounds default). Arithmetic 67.0 -> 81.8, GSM8K 77.0 -> 85.0, chess move validity 29.3 -> 45.2, biography factuality 66.0 -> 73.8, MMLU 63.9 -> 71.1; single-agent reflection helped less or hurt (MMLU 63.9 -> 57.7). Performance rises monotonically with more agents and rounds (plateau around 4 rounds); summarizing peer answers instead of concatenating improves results and enables 5+ agents.
papers.design_implication: Debate is a useful diversity-plus-reconciliation mechanism for open-ended or judgment tasks, but it costs agents x rounds calls; summarize peer outputs to control context, cap at 3 agents x 2 rounds, and compare against equal-budget self-consistency (Huang et al.) before adoption.

papers.title: Encouraging Divergent Thinking in Large Language Models through Multi-Agent Debate
papers.authors: Tian Liang, Zhiwei He, Wenxiang Jiao, Xing Wang, Yan Wang, Rui Wang, Yujiu Yang, Shuming Shi, Zhaopeng Tu
papers.citation_signal: EMNLP 2024 main; widely cited MAD framework
papers.key_contribution: Identifies the Degeneration-of-Thought problem in self-reflection (a confident model stops generating new ideas even when wrong) and proposes tit-for-tat debate with a judge. Finds that adaptive termination and a modest disagreement level are both required, and that a judge sharing a model with one debater is not fair.
papers.design_implication: If debate is used, terminate adaptively on convergence, keep disagreement prompts moderate, and use a judge from a different model family than the debaters.

papers.title: Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems
papers.authors: Karl Cobbe, Vineet Kosaraju, Mohammad Bavarian, Mark Chen, Heewoo Jun, Lukasz Kaiser, Matthias Plappert, Jerry Tworek, Jacob Hilton, Reiichiro Nakano, Christopher Hesse, John Schulman
papers.citation_signal: 11,240 citations (Semantic Scholar, Oct 2026); introduced GSM8K and the verifier/best-of-N paradigm
papers.key_contribution: Introduces GSM8K (8.5K problems) and trains verifiers to score completions; at test time 100 completions are sampled and the top-ranked is returned. 6B verification slightly outperforms a finetuned 175B model (~30x model-size equivalent). Token-level verifiers train slower but outperform solution-level ones, which overfit (dropout mitigates). Verifier performance improves up to ~400 completions then declines; voting among the top 3-5 verifier-ranked solutions is best at 100 samples (~top 30 at 3,200).
papers.design_implication: A small trained verifier plus best-of-N is a cost-effective substitute for a larger generator. Combine verifier ranking with majority vote over the top few (verifier-weighted voting), and expect diminishing or negative returns past a few hundred samples.

papers.title: Let's Verify Step by Step
papers.authors: Hunter Lightman, Vineet Kosaraju, Yura Burda, Harri Edwards, Bowen Baker, Teddy Lee, Jan Leike, John Schulman, Ilya Sutskever, Karl Cobbe
papers.citation_signal: Several thousand citations; defining process reward model paper; releases PRM800K
papers.key_contribution: Process supervision (step-level labels) beats outcome supervision: at N=1860 best-of-N on MATH, PRM 78.2% vs ORM 72.4% vs majority vote 69.6%, with the PRM gap widening as N grows. Step scores aggregated by product (78.2%) or minimum (77.6%) perform similarly. PRM800K: ~800K step labels on 75K solutions. Active learning (labelling convincing wrong answers) is ~2.6x more data-efficient. Out-of-distribution STEM exams: PRM 72.9% vs ORM 63.8% vs majority 61.3%.
papers.design_implication: When a verifier can be trained for the domain, label at the step level and aggregate with min or product; a PRM generalizes better than an ORM and scales with more samples where majority vote plateaus. Collect labels by targeting confident-but-wrong outputs.

papers.title: Making Large Language Models Better Reasoners with Step-Aware Verifier (DiVeRSe)
papers.authors: Yifei Li, Zeqi Lin, Shizhuo Zhang, Qiang Fu, Bei Chen, Jian-Guang Lou, Weizhu Chen
papers.citation_signal: Several hundred citations; early verifier-weighted voting method
papers.key_contribution: Combines diverse prompts (diverse reasoning paths), a verifier used for weighted voting, and step-level verification. With code-davinci-002, GSM8K rises 74.4% -> 83.2% and new SOTA on 6 of 8 reasoning benchmarks.
papers.design_implication: Weighted voting (verifier score as vote weight) dominates both plain majority vote and plain top-1 verifier selection; diversify prompts, not just temperature, to decorrelate samples.

papers.title: Math-Shepherd: Verify and Reinforce LLMs Step-by-step without Human Annotations
papers.authors: Peiyi Wang, Lei Li, Zhihong Shao, R.X. Xu, Damai Dai, Yifei Li, Deli Chen, Y. Wu, Zhifang Sui
papers.citation_signal: Several hundred citations; standard recipe for automatic PRM labels
papers.key_contribution: Builds a PRM with automatically constructed step labels (Monte Carlo completions from each step: a step is good if some continuation reaches the correct answer). Used for reranking and step-level PPO: Mistral-7B GSM8K 77.9 -> 84.1 (PPO) and 89.1 with verification; MATH 28.6 -> 33.0 and 43.5.
papers.design_implication: Step-level verifier labels can be produced without humans whenever a final-answer oracle exists (unit tests, reference values, simulator outputs), which makes PRMs feasible for engineering domains.

papers.title: Rewarding Progress: Scaling Automated Process Verifiers for LLM Reasoning
papers.authors: Amrith Setlur, Chirag Nagpal, Adam Fisch, Xinyang Geng, Jacob Eisenstein, Rishabh Agarwal, Alekh Agarwal, Jonathan Berant, Aviral Kumar
papers.citation_signal: Google DeepMind / CMU; influential on PRM design
papers.key_contribution: Defines process reward as progress (change in probability of eventual success before vs after a step), measured under a separate prover policy. Process advantage verifiers (PAVs) are >8% more accurate and 1.5-5x more compute-efficient than ORMs for test-time search, and give 5-6x sample-efficiency gains in online RL.
papers.design_implication: Train step verifiers to predict progress rather than absolute correctness, and allow a weaker prover to label progress for a stronger generator; this reduces search compute for the same accuracy.

papers.title: Generative Verifiers: Reward Modeling as Next-Token Prediction
papers.authors: Lunjun Zhang, Arian Hosseini, Hritik Bansal, Mehran Kazemi, Aviral Kumar, Rishabh Agarwal
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2025; widely cited generative-verifier paradigm
papers.key_contribution: Trains verifiers with next-token prediction jointly on verification and solution generation, enabling CoT verification and majority voting over verification rationales. Best-of-N gains over discriminative verifiers: algorithmic tasks 5% -> 45.3%, GSM8K 73% -> 93.4%, MATH easy-to-hard 28% -> 44.6%, MMLU abstract algebra 37.9% -> 53.5%; synthetic rationales suffice.
papers.design_implication: A verifier that reasons (and can itself be sampled and voted) outperforms a scalar classifier; implement the verifier interface so it can return a rationale plus a probability, and allow k verifier samples for hard cases.

papers.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
papers.authors: Charlie Snell, Jaehoon Lee, Kelvin Xu, Aviral Kumar
papers.citation_signal: Highly cited (Google DeepMind / Berkeley); foundational for compute-optimal verification
papers.key_contribution: Studies PRM-guided search (best-of-N, beam, lookahead) and sequential revision. A compute-optimal, difficulty-adaptive allocation improves test-time scaling efficiency by more than 4x over best-of-N; FLOPs-matched, test-time compute beats a 14x larger model on problems where the base model has non-trivial success rates.
papers.design_implication: Estimate query difficulty (e.g., from PRM scores or sample agreement) and allocate verification budget per query: cheap verification for easy inputs, search/PRM for medium, and escalation/abstention for very hard ones where extra compute does not help.

papers.title: Large Language Models are Better Reasoners with Self-Verification
papers.authors: Yixuan Weng, Minjun Zhu, Fei Xia, Bin Li, Shizhu He, Shengping Liu, Bin Sun, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
papers.citation_signal: Findings of EMNLP 2023; several hundred citations
papers.key_contribution: Backward verification: treat the candidate conclusion as a given condition and check that the original problem's facts can be re-derived (e.g., mask a known quantity and predict it). Produces interpretable verification scores used to select among CoT candidates; improves arithmetic, commonsense and logical reasoning.
papers.design_implication: For quantitative engineering outputs (dimensions, tolerances, load calculations), implement backward checks: substitute the proposed result back into the constraints and verify the inputs are recovered.

papers.title: Deductive Verification of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.authors: Zhan Ling, Yunhao Fang, Xuanlin Li, Zhiao Huang, Mingu Lee, Roland Memisevic, Hao Su
papers.citation_signal: NeurIPS 2023; several hundred citations
papers.key_contribution: Verifying a whole deductive chain at once is unreliable even for ChatGPT; decomposing verification into step-level subprocesses that see only their required premises (Natural Program format) makes verification more reliable and improves answer correctness.
papers.design_implication: Verify reasoning step by step with a minimal premise context per step rather than one holistic pass; structure generator outputs so each step cites the premises it depends on.

papers.title: CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests
papers.authors: Bei Chen, Fengji Zhang, Anh Nguyen, Daoguang Zan, Zeqi Lin, Jian-Guang Lou, Weizhu Chen
papers.citation_signal: Several hundred citations; basis of execution-based selection in code tools
papers.key_contribution: Generates test cases with the same model, executes every candidate against them, and ranks by dual execution agreement (agreement with tests and with other candidates producing the same outputs). HumanEval pass@1 65.8%, +18.8 absolute over code-davinci-002 and >20 points over prior SOTA; validated on HumanEval, MBPP, APPS, CodeContests.
papers.design_implication: For any executable artifact (code, SQL, config, CAD scripts), generate tests plus candidates, execute, and cluster candidates by output signature; pick the largest cluster that passes the most tests. This is the strongest, cheapest verifier available for engineering code.

papers.title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
papers.authors: Saurav Kadavath, Tom Conerly, Amanda Askell, et al. (Anthropic)
papers.citation_signal: Over a thousand citations; foundational calibration/self-evaluation study
papers.key_contribution: Large models are well-calibrated on multiple-choice/true-false in the right format; P(True) self-evaluation of a proposed answer is informative and improves when the model sees many of its own samples before judging one; models can be trained to predict P(IK) (that they know the answer) with partial cross-task generalization, and P(IK) rises appropriately when relevant source material is in context.
papers.design_implication: Elicit P(True) after showing the model several alternative samples (not in isolation), and expect calibration to depend on format; use P(True) as one input to the confidence fusion rather than the sole gate.

papers.title: Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback
papers.authors: Katherine Tian, Eric Mitchell, Allan Zhou, Archit Sharma, Rafael Rafailov, Huaxiu Yao, Chelsea Finn, Christopher D. Manning
papers.citation_signal: EMNLP 2023; several hundred citations; standard reference for verbalized confidence
papers.key_contribution: For RLHF models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude), verbalized confidences are better calibrated than conditional probabilities on TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA, often halving ECE. Best is one-stage verbalized top-k (k=4): GPT-4 ECE 0.041/0.056/0.198 vs label-probability 0.078/0.219/0.445; GPT-3.5 0.054/0.065/0.203 vs 0.140/0.256/0.451. Numeric probabilities match or beat linguistic phrases; CoT does not consistently help; temperature scaling helps further.
papers.design_implication: Elicit confidence by asking for top-k (k=4) candidate answers with numeric probabilities in one call, then calibrate with temperature scaling on a held-out set; do not rely on raw token probabilities from RLHF models.

papers.title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
papers.authors: Miao Xiong, Zhiyuan Hu, Xinyang Lu, Yifei Li, Jie Fu, Junxian He, Bryan Hooi
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2024; several hundred citations
papers.key_contribution: Black-box framework = prompting strategy x sampling x aggregation. LLMs are systematically overconfident when verbalizing; larger models calibrate better; human-inspired prompts, multi-sample consistency and better aggregation reduce overconfidence; white-box methods are only modestly better (AUROC 0.522 -> 0.605 example). No single technique wins everywhere and all struggle on professional-knowledge tasks.
papers.design_implication: Fuse verbalized confidence with sample-consistency (hybrid aggregation) and recalibrate per domain; expect poor calibration on specialized engineering knowledge and compensate with retrieval grounding and human escalation thresholds.

papers.title: A Survey on LLM-as-a-Judge
papers.authors: Jiawei Gu, Xuhui Jiang, Zhichao Shi, et al.
papers.citation_signal: Widely cited survey with companion benchmark and awesome-list
papers.key_contribution: Organizes reliability strategies for LLM judges (consistency improvement, bias mitigation, scenario adaptation), proposes methodologies and a benchmark for evaluating judge reliability, and catalogs applications and open challenges.
papers.design_implication: Use its taxonomy as the checklist for the judge sub-module: consistency (multi-sample, swap), bias controls (position, length, self-preference), and scenario adaptation (domain rubrics, references).

papers.title: Reduce hallucinations (Claude Developer Platform documentation)
papers.authors: Anthropic
papers.citation_signal: Official vendor guidance defining state of practice
papers.key_contribution: Basic strategies: explicitly allow 'I don't know'; for documents >20K tokens extract word-for-word quotes before the task; verify with citations and retract any claim without a supporting quote. Advanced: chain-of-thought verification via thinking blocks, best-of-N verification (run the prompt multiple times and compare for inconsistencies), iterative refinement, and external-knowledge restriction (use only provided documents). Caveat: these reduce but do not eliminate hallucinations; validate critical information.
papers.design_implication: Encode these as default prompt policies in the generator-facing side of the verifier: quote-first grounding for long contexts, mandatory retraction of unsupported claims, abstention permission, and closed-book restriction for RAG, with best-of-N consistency as the cheap first-line check.

papers.title: Building effective agents
papers.authors: Anthropic (Erik Schluntz, Barry Zhang)
papers.citation_signal: Widely adopted industry reference for agent/workflow patterns
papers.key_contribution: Defines workflow patterns: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization (sectioning and voting), orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer. Evaluator-optimizer is one LLM generating while another evaluates in a loop, recommended when clear evaluation criteria exist and iteration adds measurable value (e.g., translation critique, deciding whether more search is needed). Voting runs the same task multiple times with different prompts, e.g., several reviewers flagging code vulnerabilities, or content screening with different vote thresholds to trade false positives/negatives.
papers.design_implication: Expose the verifier both as an evaluator in an evaluator-optimizer loop (with a separate model) and as a voting aggregator over parallel reviewers with configurable thresholds; this is the industry-standard integration surface.

techniques.name: Adaptive Self-Consistency (sample-vote with early stopping)
techniques.description: 1) Canonicalize the task so a final answer is extractable (number, label, SQL result set, test verdict, normalized JSON). 2) Sample reasoning paths at T~0.7 (top-k 40 or top-p 0.95), in batches of b (e.g., 3), using diverse prompt variants to decorrelate samples. 3) After each batch, canonicalize answers and compute the posterior probability that the current majority answer is stable (Adaptive-Consistency: Dirichlet/beta posterior over answer counts; stop when P(majority stays top) >= threshold). 4) Stop at threshold or k_max; return majority answer and confidence = agreement fraction (and the posterior). 5) If agreement < c_low, flag as uncertain and route to heavier verification (retrieval/tool) or abstain.
source_titles: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning and Coding with LLMs
Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
techniques.when_to_use: Any task with a canonicalizable answer: numeric/engineering calculations, classification (severity, root-cause category), extraction fields, SQL/code with executable result, multiple-choice compliance checks.
techniques.tradeoffs: Cost scales with k (k LLM calls); gains saturate quickly (5-10 paths capture most). Fails when errors are systematic (all samples share the same misconception) and when answers cannot be normalized. Provides the cheapest reliable confidence signal; at equal budget it beats multi-agent debate (Huang et al.).
techniques.default_parameters: k_min=3, k_max=10 (up to 40 for high-stakes), batch=3, temperature 0.7, stopping threshold 0.95 posterior (Adaptive-Consistency reports up to 7.9x fewer samples with <0.1% accuracy loss), low-agreement trigger c_low=0.6. Self-Consistency used 40 paths and found saturation by 5-10.

techniques.name: Universal Self-Consistency / LLM-selected consensus for free-form outputs
techniques.description: 1) Generate n candidates (T~0.7). 2) Build a single selection prompt listing candidates in randomized order with index labels, asking the model to identify the response most consistent with the majority and output only its index (optionally with a short rationale). 3) Run the selection 2-3 times with shuffled orders; take the modal selection. 4) Return the selected candidate; because USC yields no confidence, attach confidence from a separate estimator (semantic entropy over the candidates or verbalized confidence).
source_titles: Universal Self-Consistency for Large Language Model Generation
Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
techniques.when_to_use: Summaries, specifications, incident narratives, design rationales, code where execution is unavailable; whenever majority vote cannot be computed.
techniques.tradeoffs: One extra long-context call; candidates limited by context window; consistency != quality (oracle 96.2 vs USC 90.2 on GSM8K); selection has position bias so order must be randomized; gains plateau around 5 candidates and can drop at 16.
techniques.default_parameters: n=5-8 candidates (paper default 8; summarization gains flat after 5), 2-3 shuffled selection passes, selection at temperature 0, cap total candidate tokens at ~50% of context window.

techniques.name: Discrete Semantic Entropy / SelfCheckGPT hallucination scoring
techniques.description: 1) Produce the primary answer (T=0 or low). 2) Sample N stochastic answers (T=1.0). 3) For short answers: cluster the N samples by bidirectional entailment using an NLI model (DeBERTa-large-MNLI) or an LLM judge; compute discrete semantic entropy H = -sum_c (n_c/N) log(n_c/N) over clusters. 4) For long answers: split the primary answer into sentences or atomic claims; for each, compute SelfCheck-NLI score = mean over samples of P(contradiction | sample, claim) (or generate a question per claim, sample answers, and compute semantic entropy per claim); aggregate per passage by mean and max. 5) Threshold: claims above tau are marked unsupported and routed to retrieval verification or flagged; passage score drives abstention.
source_titles: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy
Semantic Uncertainty: Linguistic Invariances for Uncertainty Estimation in Natural Language Generation
SelfCheckGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection for Generative Large Language Models
techniques.when_to_use: Black-box or API models without trustworthy logprobs; open-domain or long-form generation where no reference exists; triage before expensive retrieval checks; detecting confabulation on long-tail entities (part numbers, obscure clauses).
techniques.tradeoffs: N extra generations per query plus O(N^2) NLI pairs for clustering (cheap with a small NLI model). Detects arbitrary confabulations, not consistent misconceptions. NLI variant is nearly as strong as LLM-prompt variant at far lower cost (92.5 vs 93.4 AUC-PR).
techniques.default_parameters: N=10 samples for semantic entropy (Nature paper), N=20 for SelfCheckGPT; sampling T=1.0; NLI = DeBERTa-large-MNLI with bidirectional entailment required for same-cluster; threshold tau tuned on a labelled dev set to the desired recall of hallucinated claims (target AUROC ~0.79 reported on sentence-length tasks); passage aggregation = mean of sentence scores.

techniques.name: Factored Chain-of-Verification with minimal revision
techniques.description: 1) Draft response. 2) Plan: generate verification questions covering each factual claim (one per atomic claim). 3) Execute factored: answer each question in an isolated call that does NOT include the draft (prevents copying hallucinations); optionally route each question to retrieval or a tool instead of the model's memory (Self-Ask style). 4) Cross-check (factor+revise): for each (claim, verified answer) pair, an explicit consistency call labels agree/contradict/unknown. 5) Revise: edit only contradicted or unsupported claims with the smallest change that restores support (RARR edit budget); drop or hedge if no support is found. 6) Report claim count before/after so recall loss is visible.
source_titles: Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in Large Language Models
RARR: Researching and Revising What Language Models Say, Using Language Models
Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models (Self-Ask)
Verify-and-Edit: A Knowledge-Enhanced Chain-of-Thought Framework
techniques.when_to_use: Long-form factual outputs: specification summaries, standards interpretations, incident reports, BOM descriptions, status write-ups; especially when uncertainty signals (low agreement, high semantic entropy) are raised.
techniques.tradeoffs: Cost grows with the number of claims (one or more calls each); may reduce recall (CoVe fact count 16.6 -> 12.3); without tools it only removes what the model can recognize as wrong. Factored variants cost more than joint but are markedly more accurate.
techniques.default_parameters: One verification question per atomic claim, max 10-15 questions per response (batch beyond that); verification calls at T=0 without the draft in context; use 2-step/factored not joint; edit acceptance requires preservation >= 0.8 on a Levenshtein-ratio (RARR rejects oversized edits); trigger only when agreement < 0.6 or semantic entropy above tau (Verify-and-Edit).

techniques.name: Atomic-claim attribution scoring with tool routing (FActScore/FacTool/ALCE)
techniques.description: 1) Decompose output into atomic claims (LLM, few-shot). 2) Classify each claim by type (textual fact, numeric/arithmetic, code behavior, citation/reference, standard clause, catalog attribute). 3) Route: textual -> hybrid retrieval (BM25 + dense) over the corpus, top-5 chunks; numeric -> calculator/Python recompute; code -> execute generated tests; citation -> metadata lookup (doc registry, Scholar, PLM/ERP API); clause -> fetch the exact clause text. 4) Entailment: an NLI model or LLM labels Supported/Contradicted/No-evidence per claim given the evidence. 5) Score: attribution precision = supported/total, citation recall = fraction of claims with at least one entailing cited chunk, citation precision = fraction of citations that entail something; report with claim count and abstention rate. 6) Gate: block or revise if precision < p_min or any Contradicted claims exist.
source_titles: FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation
FacTool: Factuality Detection in Generative AI -- A Tool Augmented Framework for Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Scenarios
Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations (ALCE)
Reduce hallucinations (Claude Developer Platform documentation)
techniques.when_to_use: All RAG outputs and any output making checkable factual, numeric, or code claims; compliance-sensitive engineering documents.
techniques.tradeoffs: Most expensive family (decomposition + retrieval + entailment per claim) but highest precision; quality bounded by retriever coverage (claims about undocumented facts become No-evidence, not Contradicted); FActScore is precision-only and can be gamed by brevity.
techniques.default_parameters: Top-5 evidence passages per claim (RARR used 5 pages/query, up to 5 snippets in the report); NLI threshold for 'Supported' at P(entail) >= 0.5 with bidirectional check for equivalence claims; gate p_min = 0.9 for engineering documentation, 1.0 (no Contradicted) for compliance; FActScore estimator error <2% vs humans; always report abstention % and mean claims per response.

techniques.name: Debiased, reference-guided LLM-as-judge (pairwise and rubric)
techniques.description: Pairwise: 1) Present candidates A/B with a task-specific rubric; 2) ask for step-by-step evaluation then a verdict; 3) run again with A/B swapped; 4) only count a win if both orders agree, else tie; 5) use a judge from a different model family than the generator; 6) apply a length-controlled correction (regress out length difference) or instruct explicitly to ignore length and penalize padding. Rubric scoring (G-Eval): 1) define criteria and auto-generated evaluation steps; 2) form-fill a 1-5 score; 3) compute expected score from token probabilities or average over 5-10 samples; 4) when a reference exists (executed result, gold spec, oracle value), use reference-guided grading. Judge calibration: maintain a human-labelled anchor set and track agreement; escalate items with high position-diversity entropy to humans.
source_titles: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment
Length-Controlled AlpacaEval: A Simple Way to Debias Automatic Evaluators
LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
Prometheus: Inducing Fine-grained Evaluation Capability in Language Models
techniques.when_to_use: Selecting among free-form candidates, quality gating of documents, scoring against domain rubrics (clarity, completeness, standards compliance), and as the cheap pre-filter before expensive tool checks.
techniques.tradeoffs: 2x calls for swap, ~4x for few-shot judging; ~85% agreement with experts at best; biased on math/reasoning without references (70% failure default, 15% reference-guided); prefers LLM-style and verbose text; self-preference if same family.
techniques.default_parameters: Always 2 orderings; few-shot judge only for high-value items (+12.5 points consistency at 4x cost); rubric score as probability-weighted expectation over 1-5; 5 judge samples at T=0.7 averaged if logprobs unavailable; length-control via GLM fit on >=200 pairs; cross-family judge mandatory; human anchor set >= 100 items refreshed quarterly.

techniques.name: Verifier-guided Best-of-N with process reward models and weighted voting
techniques.description: 1) Generate N candidate solutions with step-delimited reasoning. 2) Score each step with a PRM (trained on human step labels like PRM800K, or automatic labels via Math-Shepherd-style Monte Carlo rollouts, or progress/advantage labels via PAVs); aggregate per solution with min or product of step scores. 3) Weighted vote: group candidates by canonical final answer and sum PRM scores per group (DiVeRSe/Cobbe top-k voting); return the top group's best-scoring solution. 4) Use the PRM score distribution to estimate difficulty and adapt N (Snell et al.): small N for confidently-high scores, larger N or beam search for mid-range, escalate when all scores are low. 5) Optionally use a generative verifier that emits a rationale and P(correct), and sample it k times for hard items.
source_titles: Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems
Let's Verify Step by Step
Making Large Language Models Better Reasoners with Step-Aware Verifier (DiVeRSe)
Math-Shepherd: Verify and Reinforce LLMs Step-by-step without Human Annotations
Rewarding Progress: Scaling Automated Process Verifiers for LLM Reasoning
Generative Verifiers: Reward Modeling as Next-Token Prediction
Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
techniques.when_to_use: High-volume, well-defined reasoning domains with a correctness oracle for training data (calculations, structured analysis, code with tests, requirement-to-test tracing) where a dedicated verifier can be trained or an open PRM reused.
techniques.tradeoffs: Requires training data and MLOps for the verifier; N generations per query; verifier performance can degrade beyond a few hundred samples (Cobbe); PRM generalization is better than ORM but still domain-sensitive; large gains (PRM 78.2 vs majority 69.6 at N=1860; GenRM GSM8K 73 -> 93.4).
techniques.default_parameters: N=16-64 in production (paper regimes 100-1860); aggregation = min of step scores (77.6%) or product (78.2%); weighted vote over top 3-5 verifier-ranked candidates (Cobbe); difficulty buckets by max PRM score (e.g., >0.9 easy: N=4; 0.5-0.9: N=16-32; <0.5: escalate); active learning on confident-wrong samples (~2.6x label efficiency).

techniques.name: Tool-grounded verify-and-repair loop (execution, tests, retrieval)
techniques.description: 1) Generate candidate artifact(s) and, separately, verification tests/queries (CodeT: generate test cases; FacTool: generate queries). 2) Execute: run tests in a sandbox, re-compute numbers, query retrieval/APIs. 3) Score by dual execution agreement: candidates that pass the same generated tests and produce identical outputs cluster together; rank clusters by (tests passed x cluster size). 4) If the best cluster fails required tests, repair with the concrete failure signal (stack trace, failing assertion, contradicting passage), preferring a stronger critic model for feedback; repair at most R rounds. 5) Localize before repairing: pass the failing test/step location explicitly (Tyen et al.). 6) Stop when tests pass or R reached; if still failing, abstain/escalate.
source_titles: CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests
CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
techniques.when_to_use: Code, SQL, configuration, CAD/parametric scripts, calculations, anything with an executable or queryable oracle; also factual QA with a retrievable corpus.
techniques.tradeoffs: Needs sandboxing and tool infrastructure; generated tests can be wrong (mitigated by dual agreement); repair rounds have diminishing returns (0.97-1.05x baseline at equal budget for GPT-4 on APPS); without tools the loop regresses (CRITIC ablation).
techniques.default_parameters: Candidates n=10, generated tests t=10-20 per task, repair rounds R<=2 (Olausson: breadth beats depth), repair only on external failure signals, feedback from a stronger or different model when available (repair success 4.7% -> 11.5% with GPT-4 feedback), sandbox timeout per execution 10-30 s.

techniques.name: Confidence elicitation, fusion and abstention gating
techniques.description: 1) Verbalized confidence: in one call, ask for top-k candidate answers each with a numeric probability (k=4); take the top candidate's probability. 2) Consistency confidence: agreement fraction from self-consistency or 1 - normalized semantic entropy. 3) P(True): show the model several of its own samples and ask P(True) for the chosen one (Kadavath). 4) Fuse by logistic regression or isotonic regression trained on a labelled dev set (features: verbalized p, agreement, entropy, verifier score, retrieval support fraction); apply temperature scaling. 5) Gate: release if fused p >= p_release; run heavier verification if p_mid <= p < p_release; abstain/escalate to human if p < p_mid. 6) Monitor ECE, Brier and AUROC of the fused score weekly and recalibrate.
source_titles: Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback
Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
techniques.when_to_use: Every verified output should carry a calibrated confidence for routing, SLA-based escalation and audit; essential when the pipeline must decide between answering, retrieving more, or deferring to an engineer.
techniques.tradeoffs: Verbalized confidence alone is overconfident and weak on professional-knowledge tasks; consistency needs extra samples; calibration drifts across model versions and domains and must be re-fit; fused scores are only as good as the labelled calibration set.
techniques.default_parameters: Verbalized 1-stage top-k with k=4 and numeric probabilities (Tian: ECE ~0.04-0.06 on TriviaQA/SciQ for GPT-4 vs 0.08-0.22 for label probabilities); temperature scaling on >=500 labelled items; default thresholds p_release=0.85, p_mid=0.5 (tune to cost of error); target ECE <= 0.05 and AUROC >= 0.8 for failure prediction.

techniques.name: Multi-agent debate with summarization and adaptive termination
techniques.description: 1) Instantiate A agents (ideally different models or prompts) that each answer independently. 2) Each round, give every agent a summary (not concatenation) of the other agents' current answers and ask it to update or defend with reasons. 3) Terminate when answers converge (all agree) or after R rounds. 4) A judge from a different model family (or majority vote if canonicalizable) produces the final answer. 5) Always benchmark against adaptive self-consistency at matched call count before enabling in production.
source_titles: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
Encouraging Divergent Thinking in Large Language Models through Multi-Agent Debate
Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
techniques.when_to_use: Open-ended judgment tasks (design trade-off reviews, root-cause hypotheses, risk assessments) where diversity of perspective matters and no oracle exists; red-team style review of a plan.
techniques.tradeoffs: Cost = A x R calls plus summaries; at equal budget underperforms self-consistency on canonicalizable tasks (83.0 vs 88.2 on GSM8K at 9 responses); degeneration-of-thought if agents converge too early; unfair judging if judge shares a model with one debater.
techniques.default_parameters: A=3 agents, R=2 rounds (Du et al. default), max R=4 (plateau), summarize peer answers when A>=3, adaptive stop on unanimous agreement, cross-family judge, moderate 'tit-for-tat' disagreement prompt.

architecture_recommendations: 1. Expose a single Verifier interface: verify(task_prompt, candidates[], context{evidence, tools, rubric, reference?}, policy) -> VerificationReport{selected_candidate, per_claim_verdicts, fused_confidence, cost, trace}. Make the component stateless between calls and pluggable at any pipeline stage (post-retrieval, post-generation, post-decomposition merge).

2. Put a planner in front: an LLM 'verification strategist' reads the natural-language task prompt and the candidate(s), classifies the output type (canonicalizable answer, executable artifact, long-form factual, subjective/stylistic, mixed) and the available oracles (tests, retrieval corpus, calculator, reference answer), then emits a verification plan as structured JSON selecting strategies from a registry (adaptive-SC, USC, semantic entropy, CoVe, attribution scoring, judge, PRM best-of-N, tool loop, debate) with budgets. Policies can override or pin the plan per domain.

3. Implement a Strategy Registry where each strategy declares: applicability predicate (needs canonical answer? needs tools?), cost model (calls, tokens, latency), and output schema (score, verdicts, confidence). New domains add strategies or claim-type routers without touching the core.

4. Make 'external evidence first' the ordering rule: execution/tests and retrieval entailment are terminal authorities; LLM judgment is advisory; intrinsic self-critique is never allowed to override an unverified draft (Huang et al., CRITIC ablation, Kamoi et al.). Encode this as a precedence table in config.

5. Use an atomic Claim as the unit of verification. A Claim has {text, type, span, evidence[], verdict, confidence, verifier_used}. Long outputs are decomposed once and claims are verified in parallel; the report aggregates precision, citation recall, contradiction count, claim count and abstention so brevity gaming is visible.

6. Implement claim-type routing with pluggable tool adapters: retrieval (hybrid), code sandbox, calculator/units engine, document/clause fetcher, catalog/PLM/ERP lookups, ticketing/incident DB, test-log parser. Each adapter returns normalized Evidence{source_id, content, timestamp, score}.

7. Confidence fusion module: collect agreement, semantic entropy, verbalized top-k probability, judge score, verifier/PRM score, retrieval support fraction; fit a calibrator (logistic/isotonic + temperature scaling) per domain on labelled data; publish ECE/AUROC; drive a three-way gate (release / escalate verification / abstain-to-human) with configurable thresholds.

8. Budget controller: per-query difficulty estimation (initial agreement or PRM score) allocates compute (Snell et al.): easy -> k=3 SC; medium -> k up to 10 + claim checks; hard -> PRM search or human escalation. Enforce hard caps on calls, tokens and wall-clock; expose cost in the report.

9. Judge sub-module with built-in debiasing: position swap, randomized ordering, length control, cross-family model selection, reference-guided mode when a reference/executed result exists, probability-weighted rubric scores, and a human-anchor calibration set with agreement monitoring and drift alerts.

10. Repair sub-module is opt-in and evidence-gated: it accepts a failing signal (test failure, contradicted claim with evidence, error location) and performs minimal edits with a preservation budget (RARR), at most 2 rounds, using a stronger or different critic model; every edit is diffed and logged.

11. Observability and audit: persist the full verification trace (prompts, samples, evidence, verdicts, scores, model versions, seeds) with the output; emit metrics (precision, abstention rate, ECE, cost per verified answer, latency P50/P95, escalation rate); support replay for incident review and regulatory audit.

12. Configuration surface per domain: rubrics, claim-type definitions, tool adapters, evidence corpora, thresholds (p_release, p_min precision, tau entropy), budgets, model roster (generator vs judge families), redaction rules. Ship presets: 'code', 'spec/requirements', 'standards-compliance', 'incident-report', 'test-log-analysis', 'BOM/CAD-metadata', 'general-QA'.

13. Safety and failure handling: default to abstention with an explicit 'insufficient evidence' message (Anthropic guidance) rather than best-effort release when gates fail; never let verification prompts ingest untrusted retrieved text as instructions (treat evidence as data); sandbox all execution with timeouts and resource limits.

14. Testing and evaluation harness: golden sets per domain with human labels, adversarial sets (verbose/padded answers, swapped-order pairs, plausible-but-wrong code), regression tests on each model upgrade, and matched-budget comparisons (SC vs debate vs judge) before enabling any new strategy.
pitfalls: Intrinsic self-correction regresses accuracy (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 89.0 after two rounds; GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1) -- Huang et al. 2023 'LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet'. Mitigation: only correct on external evidence; otherwise select (vote/verifier) or abstain.

Self-feedback fails to detect errors on correctness tasks (ChatGPT said 'everything looks good' on 94% of GSM8K items; math gain 0-0.2) -- Madaan et al. 2023 Self-Refine. Mitigation: use refinement only for stylistic/subjective quality with concrete feedback; route correctness to tools/verifiers.

Self-critique without tools gives negligible or negative gains (QA -0.03 F1; toxicity worsens 0.192 -> 0.223) -- Gou et al. 2023 CRITIC ablation. Mitigation: wire every critique to a tool/retrieval signal.

LLMs cannot localize their own reasoning errors even when they can fix them given the location -- Tyen et al. 2023. Mitigation: use trained localizers (small classifiers, PRMs, failing tests, contradiction spans) and pass locations to the repair step.

Code self-repair is often not worth its cost at equal sample budget (0.97-1.05x baseline for GPT-4 on APPS) and is bottlenecked by feedback quality -- Olausson et al. 2023. Mitigation: prefer more initial samples filtered by tests; use a stronger critic for feedback; cap repairs at 1-2.

Multi-agent debate underperforms self-consistency at equal response counts (83.0 vs 88.2 on GSM8K at 9 responses) -- Huang et al. 2023; debate can degenerate when agents converge early -- Liang et al. 2023. Mitigation: benchmark at matched budget; adaptive termination; cross-family judge.

Position bias in LLM judges (GPT-4 only 65% order-consistent; Claude-v1 23.8%; rankings flipped on 66/80 queries) -- Zheng et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2023 'Not Fair Evaluators'. Mitigation: evaluate both orders, count only consistent wins, randomize order, escalate high position-entropy items.

Verbosity bias (91.3% of GPT-3.5/Claude-v1 judgments fooled by repetitive padding) -- Zheng et al. 2023; Dubois et al. 2024. Mitigation: length-controlled regression correction, explicit anti-verbosity rubric, token caps on candidates.

Self-preference / self-enhancement bias (judges favor their own generations; strength correlates with self-recognition) -- Panickssery et al. 2024; Zheng et al. 2023; G-Eval authors flag preference for LLM text -- Liu et al. 2023. Mitigation: cross-family judges, non-LLM verifiers for final gates, human anchor sets.

Judges are unreliable graders of math/reasoning without references (70% failure with default prompt vs 15% reference-guided) -- Zheng et al. 2023; whole-chain verification is unreliable -- Ling et al. 2023. Mitigation: reference-guided or execution-grounded grading; step-wise verification with minimal premises.

Precision-only factuality metrics reward saying less (CoVe fact count 16.6 -> 12.3; FActScore ignores abstention) -- Min et al. 2023; Dhuliawala et al. 2023. Mitigation: always report claim count, abstention rate and recall-oriented coverage checks alongside precision.

Factuality collapses on rare entities (ChatGPT ~80% -> 16% FActScore for rarest entities) and later in long outputs -- Min et al. 2023. Mitigation: retrieval grounding for long-tail identifiers (part numbers, obscure clauses), shorter generation units, claim-level checks.

Verbalized confidence is overconfident and weak on professional-knowledge tasks; raw RLHF token probabilities are poorly calibrated -- Xiong et al. 2023; Tian et al. 2023. Mitigation: top-k verbalization, consistency fusion, temperature scaling, per-domain recalibration, human escalation thresholds.

Consistency is not correctness: systematic shared misconceptions pass self-consistency and USC (oracle 96.2 vs USC 90.2 on GSM8K) -- Chen et al. 2023. Mitigation: pair agreement with evidence-based checks; diversify prompts and models to decorrelate samples.

Verifier/best-of-N returns can diminish or reverse with too many samples (6B verifier declines past ~400 completions; USC GSM8K dropped at 16 samples) -- Cobbe et al. 2021; Chen et al. 2023. Mitigation: adaptive sample counts; weighted voting over top-k; difficulty-aware budgets.

Citation support is incomplete even for the best models (lack complete support 50% of the time on ELI5) -- Gao et al. 2023 ALCE. Mitigation: NLI-based citation recall/precision gating; retract unsupported claims (Anthropic guidance).

Unfair experimental baselines inflate self-correction claims (oracle labels, unequal budgets) -- Kamoi et al. 2024; Huang et al. 2023. Mitigation: internal evaluations must compare at matched cost without oracle information.
evaluation_metrics: Task accuracy / exact match of the selected answer on domain golden sets (GSM8K-style for calculations; pass@k with hidden tests for code), reported for verified vs unverified pipeline and at matched compute budget

Hallucination detection quality: AUROC and AUC-PR of the uncertainty/hallucination score for predicting incorrect claims (Farquhar et al. AUROC 0.790; SelfCheckGPT AUC-PR 93.4 as references); AURAC (area under rejection-accuracy curve) for abstention value
Attribution precision (FActScore-style supported fraction), citation recall and citation precision (ALCE NLI), contradiction rate, plus mandatory companions: claims per response and abstention rate
Preservation when revising: Levenshtein-ratio or intent-preservation judgment and F1_AP (harmonic mean of attribution and preservation, RARR)
Calibration of fused confidence: Expected Calibration Error (target <= 0.05), Brier score, reliability diagrams; failure-prediction AUROC (target >= 0.8)
Judge reliability: agreement with human experts on an anchor set (reference ~85% GPT-4 vs 81% human-human), position consistency rate after swap, length-bias slope, cross-order verdict entropy
Verifier quality (PRM/ORM): best-of-N accuracy curves vs N, step-level AUROC against labelled steps, out-of-distribution accuracy on held-out task families
Selective prediction: coverage vs accuracy curve at operating thresholds; escalation rate to humans and human-overturn rate of verifier verdicts
Cost and latency: LLM calls and tokens per verified answer, P50/P95 latency, average samples used under adaptive stopping (target >= 3x reduction vs fixed k_max), tool-execution time
Regression and robustness: accuracy on adversarial sets (verbose padding, swapped order, plausible-but-wrong code, long-tail entities), drift metrics across model versions
engineering_adaptation_notes: Code and scripts (including CAD parametric scripts, SQL, infra configs): execution is the oracle. Use CodeT-style generated tests plus dual execution agreement, static analysis and compiler output as evidence; treat 'all generated tests pass and the largest output cluster agrees' as release criteria; keep repair rounds <= 2 with the failure trace as feedback.

Specifications and requirements: decompose into atomic requirement claims; verify traceability by retrieving the parent requirement/standard clause and running entailment; check consistency across requirements (contradiction detection between claims); use rubric judges for clarity/testability (G-Eval style) with human-anchored calibration.

Standards and compliance documents: route clause claims to an exact-clause fetcher (version-pinned); require Supported verdicts with citations for every normative statement; set p_min precision to 1.0 for compliance assertions and force abstention otherwise; log the standard edition/version in the evidence record.

Numeric engineering calculations (loads, tolerances, power budgets, unit conversions): recompute with a calculator/units library (FacTool math arm), apply backward verification (substitute result into constraints, Weng et al.), and use self-consistency over independent derivations; flag unit mismatches as Contradicted.

Test logs and telemetry: ground every claim in parsed log lines (regex/structured parsers as a tool adapter); verify counts, timestamps and error codes by direct lookup rather than LLM reading; use semantic entropy to detect speculative root-cause statements and mark them as hypotheses.

Incident reports and postmortems: separate facts (timeline, metrics, config changes) from hypotheses; facts must be attributed to tickets, alerts or log evidence; hypotheses get explicit confidence and are candidates for multi-agent debate review; enforce preservation budgets so verification does not rewrite the responder's narrative.

CAD/BOM metadata: part numbers, revisions, suppliers and quantities are long-tail identifiers where LLM recall is weakest (FActScore rare-entity collapse); always verify against PLM/ERP APIs; treat any unverifiable identifier as a blocking Contradicted/No-evidence claim.

Domain verifiers: where final-answer oracles exist (tests, reference values, simulators), build Math-Shepherd-style automatic step labels to train small PRMs/localizers for design-review and calculation chains; use them for weighted best-of-N and error localization before any LLM repair.

Human-in-the-loop: expose position-entropy, fused-confidence and contradiction flags as escalation triggers to engineers; capture their adjudications to grow the calibration and PRM training sets (active learning on confident-but-wrong items, ~2.6x label efficiency per Lightman et al.).

Security: retrieved documents, logs and tool outputs are untrusted data; verification prompts must quarantine them as evidence blocks, and sandboxed execution must have no network or credential access.
composition_notes: Hybrid retrieval: the verifier is the primary consumer of retrieval for claim-level evidence (top-5 passages per claim with BM25+dense fusion) and the primary producer of retrieval feedback: No-evidence verdicts and low citation recall indicate retriever gaps; Verify-and-Edit shows agreement-triggered retrieval, so run expensive re-retrieval only for low-consistency outputs. Attribution scoring (ALCE/FActScore) doubles as the RAG grounding gate.

Task decomposition: decomposition produces sub-tasks with canonicalizable outputs, which makes self-consistency and step-wise verification (Ling et al., Lightman et al.) applicable per sub-task; verification should run at sub-task boundaries and at the recomposition step (compositionality gap, Press et al.), and the decomposer should emit verification hints (expected type, oracle availability) for the planner.

Answer verification itself: strategies compose in layers -- cheap sampling/agreement first, then claim-level evidence checks, then judge/debate for residual subjective quality, with confidence fusion as the single output; the precedence rule 'external evidence over LLM judgment over self-critique' must hold across layers.

Parallelization: sampling k paths, verifying claims, running both judge orderings, executing generated tests and debating agents are all embarrassingly parallel; implement them as fan-out/fan-in with the adaptive stopping criterion applied across batches (Adaptive-Consistency) and the budget controller enforcing caps. Anthropic's voting pattern (parallel reviewers with vote thresholds) is the direct integration surface.

Caching: cache canonicalized sample answers and claim verdicts keyed by (model version, prompt hash, evidence hash) so repeated questions skip re-verification; cache NLI/entailment results per (claim, passage) pair and executed test results per (code hash, test hash); invalidate on corpus or model version change; semantic caches must store the fused confidence and only serve high-confidence entries (e.g., p >= 0.85) to avoid caching hallucinations.

Pipeline RAG: in a full RAG pipeline the verifier sits after generation as the grounding gate (citation recall/precision, contradiction = 0 for compliance), feeds revision (RARR-style minimal edits) and abstention ('insufficient evidence'), and emits attribution reports; it also enables evaluator-optimizer loops (Anthropic) where the evaluator decides whether more retrieval is needed.

Prompting/architecture best practices: adopt Anthropic's hallucination-reduction defaults (permission to say 'I don't know', quote-first grounding for >20K-token contexts, cite-and-retract, closed-book restriction) in the generator so the verifier's load is lower; keep generator and judge in different model families; log everything for audit; compare any new verification strategy against adaptive self-consistency at matched cost before enabling it.
